candidateRows: Contingent reality requires an explanation beyond the entire collection of contingent things.
This establishes the explanatory principle and necessary external terminus on which the subsequent identification of a divine cause depends.

After announcing a nine-question positive case, Trent distinguishes contingent things from their explanations, defends sufficient reason, rejects an infinite contingent regress, and infers an explanation beyond the contingent universe.
The universe does not explain itself because existence is not a necessary property of universes.
Rejecting the universe as a necessary self-explanatory entity is essential to locating the required explanation outside the universe itself.

Trent contrasts a triangle's essential three-sidedness with its contingent color and argues that asking why the universe exists remains intelligible, indicating that universes do not exist by necessity.
Change requires a purely actual first actualizer rather than an infinite series of derivative actualizers.
The act-and-potency argument supplies a first cause characterized as pure actuality and excludes the changing universe from being that cause.
Trent analyzes change as potential becoming actual, argues that derivative actualizers cannot constitute a sufficient infinite series, and concludes that a purely actual cause must ground change.
An infinite past causal history is contradictory, so the universe began and requires an uncaused cause.
This supplies an independent route from the alleged impossibility of infinite causal histories to a finite past and uncaused necessary source.

Using the paper-passer scenario and related paradoxes, Trent argues that causal histories cannot be infinite, infers a finite past, and consolidates the resulting cause as necessary, uncaused, and purely actual.
The first cause must be changeless, timeless, immaterial, unlimited in power, and necessarily existent.
These deductions connect the generic first cause to several traditional divine attributes central to the affirmative case that the cause is God.

Trent derives changelessness from pure actuality, timelessness from changelessness, immateriality from transcendence of space and time, unlimited power from unrestricted actuality, and necessity from independence and incapacity for nonexistence.
The universe's cause is personal and all-knowing rather than an abstract or impersonal explanatory entity.
Personality and knowledge are indispensable to the transition from a metaphysical first cause to the traditional conception of God defended by the pro side.

Trent argues that causal efficacy excludes abstract objects, that creation from nothing calls for an agent explanation, that necessary abstract truths require a necessary mind, and that divine explanation is preferable to brute origination.
Objective moral facts support a supremely good divine source and therefore support God's existence.
The moral argument directly concludes that God exists and supplies the goodness attribute required by Trent's cumulative identification of the first cause.
Alex's previously stated account of moral truths as consequences of subjective well-being assumptions.

Trent argues that pure actuality lacks defect, presents moral realism as evidence for God, appeals to apparently objective moral truths, and challenges Alex's well-being account with a hypothetical involving engineered willing slaves.
Moral responsibility and the wrongness of punishing innocents require free will and a divine moral foundation.
The argument challenges the con speaker's determinism while reinforcing the affirmative claim that objective moral responsibility requires divine grounding.
Alex's position that physical events, including human actions, are determined by prior physical causes.

Trent contends that determinism would make blaming offenders analogous to blaming natural forces and could permit instrumental punishment of innocents, contrary to objective facts about responsibility and justice.
Apparently gratuitous animal suffering is more expected under naturalism and seriously undermines belief in a loving, just God.
Alex presents animal suffering as his principal positive reason against Christian theism and contrasts its evidential fit under theism and naturalism.

Alex argues that a loving God could permit no more suffering than necessary, uses an unseen deer's prolonged agony to press the possibility of gratuitous suffering, notes the absence of clear animal compensation, and says such suffering fits naturalism better.
Heaven would show that free will can exist without suffering, defeating the claim that freedom requires permission for grave evil.
This counterexample directly attacks a major theistic explanation of moral evil by alleging a possible realm containing freedom without corresponding suffering.
The theistic free-will defense that preventing severe moral evil would be incompatible with genuine human freedom.

Alex grants for argument that love requires freedom, then asks whether heaven contains both free will and unrestricted wrongdoing; if it contains freedom without suffering, he argues the same combination is possible on earth.
A universally sufficient explanation for every thought would entail determinism, undermining both libertarian free will and the theist's account of moral responsibility.
The argument challenges the compatibility of two major pro-side commitments: the principle of sufficient reason and morally responsible free agency.
Trent Horn's reliance on sufficient reason together with free will and moral responsibility.
Alex applies sufficient reason to the formation of particular thoughts and argues that the resulting explanatory chain becomes deterministic, creating an internal tension in Trent's case.
Quantum randomness threatens the principle of sufficient reason, while preserving realism through nonlocal interpretations carries scientific and causal costs.
This directly attacks the explanatory principle supporting the contingency argument by claiming that modern quantum results conflict with its unrestricted application.
Trent Horn's claim that rejecting sufficient reason would undermine ordinary scientific inquiry.

Alex argues that genuinely random quantum outcomes lack fully sufficient explanations and that retaining realism requires nonlocality with consequences that may themselves disrupt scientific causation.
Quantum events may have probabilistic causes, and deterministic hidden-variable interpretations show that quantum mechanics does not refute sufficient reason.
The response protects the principle of sufficient reason, a key premise in the pro side's contingency argument, from the quantum-randomness objection.
Alex O'Connor's argument that quantum randomness falsifies the principle of sufficient reason.
Trent distinguishes probabilistic from deterministic causation, appeals to experimental regularity, and notes that some interpretations of quantum mechanics posit determinate hidden causes.
A world that freely develops from imperfection toward heaven contains goods unavailable in a world whose inhabitants are created already perfected.
This is the principal pro-side answer to the heaven counterexample and explains why temporary earthly freedom and suffering might be divinely permitted.
Alex O'Connor's claim that freedom without suffering in heaven makes earthly suffering unnecessary.
Trent accepts that heaven lacks evil but argues that freely reaching that condition realizes additional relational and moral goods that immediate creation in perfection would omit.
Human agents can cause their own rational choices, and moral responsibility provides reason to affirm free will even without a complete mechanism.
The move defends free agency against the alleged deterministic implications of sufficient reason and preserves the moral argument's responsibility premise.
Alex O'Connor's contention that sufficient explanations for choices eliminate genuine free agency.
Trent answers that persons themselves can originate rational actions, compares incomplete theories of free will with incomplete accounts of consciousness, and invokes moral responsibility.
Natural evil can be permitted as a privation within a finite physical order when God derives greater goods or prevents greater evils from it.
It directly answers the debate's central evidential problem of evil by offering a general account of pain, natural processes, virtues, and divine justification.
Alex O'Connor's argument that apparently gratuitous natural suffering counts against God's existence.
Trent describes pain and death as privations within finite systems, cites their roles in animal function and virtue, and challenges Alex to supply a criterion of gratuitousness.
Animal existence can remain worthwhile despite substantial suffering, so permitting animals to exist need not be incompatible with divine goodness.
Animal suffering is an express component of the motion, and the thought experiment supplies the pro side's main reason for allowing painful animal lives.
Alex O'Connor's claim that apparently unjustified nonhuman suffering is evidence against God.
Trent asks whether an animal-only Earth should be destroyed to prevent future pain and argues that preferring continued animal life concedes that existence may justify tolerated suffering.
Statistical regularities do not explain each particular quantum outcome, while interpretations preserving sufficient reason sacrifice locality and threaten causation.
This develops the con side's principal scientific challenge to sufficient reason and directly contests the pro side's probabilistic and hidden-variable answers.
Trent Horn's appeal to probabilistic causes and hidden-variable interpretations of quantum mechanics.
Alex distinguishes explaining an outcome distribution from explaining an individual result and argues that nonlocal alternatives preserve explanation only by accepting severe causal consequences.
A limited principle requiring explanations for the existence of things rather than every event survives quantum indeterminacy and still supports a necessary being.
The distinction narrows the key premise of the contingency argument so that quantum-event objections do not reach its inference to a necessary being.
Alex O'Connor's claim that quantum outcomes and nonlocality make sufficient reason scientifically untenable.
Trent limits sufficient reason to why entities exist, allows some events to lack determinate explanations, and maintains that this narrower principle still grounds his contingency argument.
Exempting events from sufficient explanation lets the Big Bang explain the universe without itself needing a cause, undercutting the contingency argument.
The objection targets the narrowed principle designed to preserve the contingency argument and claims that the limitation instead permits an unexplained cosmic origin.
Trent Horn's distinction between explanations for existing things and explanations for particular events.
Alex grants for argument that events need no explanations, treats the Big Bang as the event producing the universe, and argues that Trent must specially justify requiring its cause.
Species-neutral atheistic morality cannot adequately explain the greater intrinsic worth ordinarily assigned to human beings over nonhuman animals.
The move directly challenges the skeptical side's moral framework and supports the theistic case by alleging that atheism cannot ground differential human worth.
Alex's earlier claim that killing animals and killing humans can receive the same necessity-based analysis.
At the opening of Trent's cross-examination, he distinguishes defensive force from intentionally killing an innocent person and uses a maritime necessity case to test Alex's account.
The evidential problem for theism arises from the extent and depth of suffering, especially suffering that appears unnecessary, rather than from suffering as such.
This formulates a principal argument against the existence of a perfectly good God and identifies unnecessary suffering as the relevant probabilistic evidence.
Trent's question whether Alex's probabilistic argument concerns every evil or only the apparently gratuitous subset.
Alex clarifies that some suffering may enable higher-order goods, but argues that a perfectly moral being should reduce suffering wherever doing so sacrifices no greater good.
Even under the theist's own conception of goodness, the possibility of less unjustified suffering creates a problem for a perfectly good creator.
The move sharpens the problem of suffering to avoid objections based on justified suffering and presses an internal critique of the theistic worldview.
Trent's objection that some suffering can be justified and his demand for an objective criterion distinguishing justified from unjustified suffering.
Alex stipulates the theist's own standard of good and argues that either less unjustified suffering is possible, which troubles theism, or none is possible, which carries a demanding commitment.
On the theistic view, no suffering is ultimately unjustified because it can serve greater goods or prevent greater evils.
This is the principal theistic defense against the evidential problem of suffering and directly denies the key category on which Alex's objection depends.
Alex's claim that the possibility of reducing unjustified suffering would place a perfectly good creator in difficulty.
Trent rejects Alex's proposed dilemma by maintaining that divine permission of suffering is justified whenever it secures greater goods or averts greater evils.
Objective moral ought-claims lack truth value, and this remains so even if God exists, because prescriptions function as commands rather than descriptive propositions.
The position directly rejects a premise of Trent's moral argument for God and supplies a metaethical reason that divine existence would not establish objective obligations.
Trent's argument that moral realism entails God and his question whether Alex accepts that conditional premise.
Alex denies that moral prescriptions are truth-apt, distinguishes descriptive goodness claims from commands expressed by ought-language, and therefore resists the moral-realism argument.
Appealing to regular natural laws does not justify animal suffering when God could have selected different laws producing less suffering.
The move targets a proposed explanation of animal suffering and argues that divine freedom over natural laws preserves the evidential challenge to perfect goodness.
Trent's explanation that animals suffer because finite organisms operating under regular natural laws need evolved pain systems.
After establishing that alternative laws are not logically impossible, Alex argues that citing the existing laws merely describes the mechanism and does not vindicate God's choice.
An omnipotent creator may permit human and animal suffering for greater goods, and finite humans need not possess epistemic access to every divine reason.
This combines a greater-good defense with an epistemic-limits argument and applies both directly to the central challenge from apparently gratuitous animal suffering.
Alex's challenge asking why a morally perfect creator would permit the actual amount of animal suffering when different laws were possible.
Trent analogizes divine permission to limited human permissions of suffering for goods, grants God wider latitude, and argues that continued animal existence can itself be valuable.
If suffering could be reduced without any countervailing harm, refusing that reduction would be morally indefensible, so theism must deny that such a feasible improvement exists.
The thought experiment isolates suffering reduction from alleged side effects and forces a consequential choice central to assessing whether actual animal suffering is gratuitous.
Trent's suggestion that an otherwise identical feasible world with less animal suffering may be impossible and requires additional information.
Alex argues that Trent must either regard the actual quantity of suffering as unchangeable or concede reason to reduce it, illustrating the latter with a harmless reduction button.
Atheistic subjectivism cannot impose universal duties in the suffering thought experiment, whereas theism can ground objective obligations to act in particular ways.
The move turns the animal-suffering exchange into a moral argument for theism by alleging that atheism lacks the objective normativity required by the objection.
Alex's claim that declining a costless opportunity to reduce animal suffering would constitute a moral travesty.
Trent contends that Alex's framework supplies only competing subjective foundations, while Trent's theistic framework permits universal facts about what agents ought to do.
The principle of sufficient reason risks begging the question because a sufficient explanation is treated as a chain that must already terminate in an ultimate brute foundation.
The objection directly attacks the explanatory principle underwriting the contingency case for God by claiming that its required terminus is assumed rather than demonstrated.

Alex analogizes contingent explanations to instrumental actualizers, argues that each dependent explanation remains incomplete, and claims that invoking sufficiency presupposes a terminating foundation.
Personal explanations involving intentions are not fundamentally distinct from scientific explanations because the relevant mental activity may itself be scientifically explicable.
The move challenges a premise used to distinguish agent explanations from physical explanations, affecting the explanatory route from contingency to a personal divine cause.
Trent's distinction between scientific explanations and personal explanations involving an agent's intentions.
After discussion of sufficient versus complete explanations, Alex argues that wanting a drink and the associated neural processes can themselves receive scientific explanation.
Reducing intentions to material brain activity fails to explain intentional aboutness and assumes a controversial philosophy of mind rejected even by many atheists.
This reply preserves the argumentative significance of personal explanation by contending that physical descriptions omit the intentional content needed to explain agency.
Alex's claim that personal intentions and desires are as scientifically explicable as physical processes.
Trent responds that material objects and neural events lack intrinsic aboutness, so a purely material account does not explain the intentional element of a person's action.

God may permissibly create a world progressing from imperfection to perfection because it realizes greater goods, virtues, freedom, and respected agency unavailable through immediate creation in heaven.
The move directly defends the compatibility of a perfectly good God with earthly evil by identifying goods allegedly unavailable in a world created immediately perfected.
Alex's earlier objection that God could have created free creatures who always choose good, as the redeemed allegedly do in heaven.
Answering why God did not create humanity directly in a sinless heavenly condition, Trent appeals to soul-making virtues and the value of freely choosing whether to follow God.
If apprehending God in heaven makes evil psychologically impossible, heavenly agents may not freely choose good; but if grave evil remains possible, the view has deeply implausible implications.
The dilemma attacks the consistency of the free-will defense by asking whether freedom requires genuine capacity for evil even in the perfected heavenly state.
Trent's claim that immediate creation in God's presence would lack valuable freedom while perfected heavenly wills consistently apprehend and choose the good.
Alex argues that either heaven psychologically coerces good action and undermines freedom, or heavenly persons retain the possibility of atrocities, which he treats as implausible.
If objective morality exists and God is perfectly moral, God would minimize objective evil, implying that the actual world contains exactly the amount of evil compatible with divine perfection.
This supplies the normative premise connecting perfect divine goodness to the observed quantity of suffering and thereby grounds the logical or evidential problem of evil.
The audience challenge to Alex's assumption that a perfectly good God must maximize pleasure or minimize unnecessary suffering among creatures.
Alex reformulates the issue in terms of objective evil: a perfectly moral being minimizes it wherever possible, so every actual evil must allegedly be unavoidable under theism.
Perfect goodness does not require minimizing evil absolutely; God may justifiably permit evil when doing so prevents greater evil or enables greater goods.
The response rejects the key moral premise of Alex's problem of evil and substitutes a justification condition based on preventing worse outcomes or realizing greater goods.
Alex's Mackie-style premise that any perfectly moral being must minimize the total amount of evil in existence.
Trent uses a universe-destroying device as a counterexample to simple evil minimization, then analogizes divine permission of evil to accepted human tradeoffs for greater goods.
Animal suffering is the principal obstacle to seriously entertaining theism, though a sound deductive argument for God could immediately overcome his present skepticism.
The move states Alex's central reason for withholding theistic belief while clarifying that his agnosticism is defeasible by a valid and sound deductive case.
Asked whether discussions with prominent theists changed him, Alex says he gained respect for their arguments and identifies animal suffering as his chief remaining barrier.
Apparent chance does not undermine sufficient reason because random events occur within an explanatory framework of existing things, causes, and stable natural regularities.
The move protects the contingency argument's explanatory principle by distinguishing chance outcomes from the absence of reasons for why entities and causal structures exist.
Alex's contention that experimentally supported quantum randomness supplies events lacking a sufficient reason or determining explanation.
Trent illustrates chance with buried treasure and falling rocks, arguing that predictable laws and causes explain the setting in which random outcomes occur and support reliable inquiry.
Ordinary chance is merely unpredictability from unknown variables, whereas quantum mechanics exhibits true randomness in which an event occurs without a determining explanation.
This distinction presents the empirical counterexample intended to defeat a universal explanatory principle essential to the contingency-based case for God.
Trent's claim that randomness is always embedded in predictable laws and sufficient reasons and therefore cannot count against the principle of sufficient reason.
Alex says the farmer and coin examples are deterministic in principle, then argues that quantum outcomes differ because even complete knowledge of prior variables would not determine them.
Quantum indeterminacy is compatible with a limited principle of sufficient reason because particles have causes of their existence even when those causes yield outcomes probabilistically.
The response narrows sufficient reason to reasons for existence and distinguishes indeterminate causation from causeless existence, preserving the contingency argument against the quantum objection.
Alex's assertion that genuine quantum randomness consists of outcomes with no determining explanation and therefore contradicts sufficient reason.
Trent argues that atomic decay explains why a beta particle exists, while probabilistic properties explain its timing; indeterminate causes need not be absent causes.
Knowledge inaccessible to human comprehension cannot count as human knowledge, while invoking inaccessible divine knowledge presupposes the very deity at issue.
The distinction limits appeals to unknowable divine reasons, a significant subsidiary issue for assessing skeptical-theist responses to evil.
Asked whether knowledge beyond human discovery can exist, Alex distinguishes human knowledge from hypothetical knowledge possessed by a divine intellect.
There are truths beyond human discovery, and necessary truths are best grounded in a necessarily existing mind that supports a divine intellect.
The move restates a mind-based grounding argument for necessary truths and uses it as affirmative evidence for a divine intellect.
Alex's preceding claim that inaccessible content cannot qualify as human knowledge and has little force in human debate.
After Alex distinguishes inaccessible human and divine knowledge, Trent argues that undiscoverable truths exist and connects necessary truths to a necessary mind.
Ontological arguments have the greatest potential to establish a necessary being, while consciousness may also furnish an unusually promising route to theism.
Alex identifies the affirmative arguments he considers most formidable, clarifying which routes to theism remain strongest under his skepticism.
In response to a closing audience question, Alex identifies rationalist ontological reasoning and arguments involving consciousness as theistic approaches with substantial potential.
Evil is the strongest atheistic challenge, but abandoning God leaves evil without ultimate vindication or compensation and does not defeat the independent case for God.
The move directly addresses the debate's principal atheistic argument while explaining why Trent regards its emotional force as insufficient to overturn theism.
The earlier atheistic argument that severe and apparently gratuitous evil counts as evidence against a perfectly good God.
Asked for atheism's most formidable argument, Trent concedes the force of evil but argues that atheism preserves the horrors while removing possible redemption.
Rejecting theism carries the cost of denying plausible causal and explanatory principles, while the debate supplied no fatal objection to the affirmative arguments.
The closing synthesis defends the cumulative affirmative case and portrays rejection of its causal, contingency, and moral foundations as theoretically costly.
Alex's earlier objections to causal finitism, sufficient reason, pure actuality, necessary being, and the proposed moral foundation.
In his closing statement, Trent argues that atheism requires rejecting sensible explanatory commitments and that his principal affirmative arguments survived the exchange.
Alex's atheistic moral framework permits deeply counterintuitive conclusions, whereas theism grounds objective morality in God as perfect goodness and humanity as created in God's image.
Objective moral grounding is one of the debate's central issues, and this move summarizes the affirmative comparative case against Alex's account.
Alex's earlier atheistic account of moral value and his responses concerning whether otherwise prohibited acts can become permissible.
Trent closes the morality portion by alleging counterintuitive implications in Alex's view and presenting divine perfect goodness as the preferable foundation.
If the arguments establish God, divine intervention and a resurrection miracle become more probable possibilities worthy of further investigation.
The inference extends the debate's affirmative conclusion to possible revelation and miracle, making it a consequential but secondary implication of theism.
Near the end of his closing, Trent draws a further implication from God's existence toward possible supernatural action, including resurrection.
Worldviews should be tested for consequences that conflict with their holders' other commitments, including moral consequences generated by positions on evil.
This methodological concession frames Alex's closing rebuttal and explains why downstream incompatibilities matter to evaluating both sides' central commitments.
Trent's closing contention that Alex's positions should be rejected because their implications conflict with common moral intuitions.
Alex agrees that beliefs should be examined through their consequences and acknowledges that a view of evil may generate unexpected moral permissions.
The principle of sufficient reason conflicts with implications of quantum mechanics and can undermine the traditional causal principles used to justify God.
The move directly attacks a principal premise of the affirmative causal case by alleging conflict with science and with the causal framework theism employs.
Trent's defense of the principle of sufficient reason and causal reasoning as sensible foundations for arguments establishing God.
Alex turns Trent's consequence-testing method against theism, arguing that sufficient reason creates scientific and causal commitments damaging to the affirmative case.
Internal consistency is only a first test of a worldview; even a coherent and mutually compatible set of beliefs must still be independently tested for truth.
The distinction prevents coherence alone from vindicating either worldview and states the further truth-directed standard governing the debate's competing systems.
After urging scrutiny of internal incompatibilities, Alex cautions that a consistently organized worldview may still be false and requires further testing.
